sentences.text: Litargosuchus was a small, slender crocodylomorph that represents an early branch of the lineage found in South Africa.
The species name leptorhynchus refers to the animal's gracile snout, and it possessed unusually elongated limbs with hind limbs slightly longer than the front ones.
Unlike modern crocodiles, Litargosuchus was a terrestrial predator capable of running.
Litargosuchus is a monotypic genus, meaning only one species is known.

The holotype fossil was discovered in 1988 by James Kitching, who was the director of the Evolutionary Studies Institute at the University of the Witwatersrand, at Eagles Crag near Barkly East in the Eastern Cape.

Kitching and Christopher Gow initially misidentified the fossils as the species Pedeticosaurus leviseuri, but Jim Clark and Hans-Dieter Sues re-described the fossils in 2002, identifying them as a new species.

The original discovery included a near-complete skull, mandible, and several postcranial bones, though the skull material of the holotype specimen has been lost and the remaining parts are stored at the Evolutionary Studies Institute.
Researchers believe Litargosuchus hunted like a wolf but likely lived a solitary life.
The genus Litargosuchus was described by researchers Jim Clark and Hans-Dieter Sues in 2002, and the type species of the genus is Litargosuchus leptorhynchus.

Litargosuchus is currently classified within the basal clade Sphenosuchidae and is accepted as a member of the crown archosaur clade, though the exact status of Litargosuchus within Sphenosuchia is uncertain due to poor understanding of the group's phylogeny.

Litargosuchus lived during the Early Jurassic period, and fossils are found exclusively in the upper Elliot Formation in South Africa, dating from 201.4 to 192.9 million years ago across the Hettangian to Sinemurian periods.
